Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
1053 AM EDT Thu Aug 27 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Adjusted precipitation chances this morning for ongoing spotty 
showers and t-storms. Current guidance suggesting a later timing 
window for potential severe weather this afternoon between 3-9pm. 
Otherwise current forecast remains on track. 

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Warm and humid conditions combined with a cold front will lead 
to severe thunderstorms across portions of the area later today. 

- 2) Turning drier this weekend, with increasingly hot and humid 
conditions for early/mid next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst
increasingly warm and humid conditions.
Still dealing with a few spotty showers and thunderstorms this 
morning as a result of a subtle jet streak within the mean upper 
level trough axis. The bulk of this activity has been confined to 
central and northeast MD with even a few blips east of 
Charlottesville, VA. Expect this spotty shower and thunderstorm 
activity to continue over the next 2-3 hrs across these areas with a 
lull into the early afternoon period before better forcing arrives. 
Any of these thunderstorms will contain 20-30 mph of wind, small, 
hail, lightning, and locally heavy rainfall. Behind this jetlet/jet 
streak, skies have already started to clear. The warm front is now 
up toward the Richmond, VA area with cold front extending from the 
OH/PA border south to areas just west of the Ohio River. 

With this clearing, expect the atmosphere to reload ahead of the 
incumbent cold frontal boundary. As it stands now, guidance has 
backed up the timing a bit heading into the late afternoon and 
period. This is due largely in part to the actual cold front being 
disjointed from the upper level trough and any KEY MESSAGE 2... 
additional pieces of shortwave energy ahead of the main boundary. 
Coverage as a result will be fairly tricky with a mashup of spotty 
to scattered storms during the afternoon transitioning into some 
organization into the evening hours as the front drops in. Latest 
HRRR, NAMnest, ARW, and even the HREF show a scattering of storms 
initiating west of Blue Ridge and along the western shore of the bay 
between 2-5pm before advancing east between 5-10pm. Damaging winds 
will be the main threat with storms today given 25-35 kts of deep 
layer shear and modest instability values up of 1000 j/kg. Moderate 
mid level lapse rates (6.5-8 C/km), strong winds in the upper 
atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also result 
in some severe level hail. As mentioned in previous forecasts, hi-
res model guidance is still depicting some decent low-level 
curvature to hodographs, especially along the MD/PA border in 
northeast MD (due to perhaps a bay breeze ahead of the front and 
shear boundary in the area) The Storm Prediction Center continues to 
mention two-percent tornado threat today should things come 
together. 

Heavy rainfall will remain a concern given multiple rounds of 
convection, especially over central and northeast MD. Given 
relatively unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could 
result in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in 
some CAMs from Baltimore, MD points northeast). No Flood Watches are 
planned at this time, but will be something to monitor given how 
things evolve this afternoon. While some showers and storms may 
linger into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding 
down after 9-10pm.

The slow moving cold front will bisect the area Friday morning while 
the mid/upper level trough lags to the west. As a result, expect 
additional showers and thunderstorms during the peak heating period, 
especially along and south of the front. Highest probabilities for 
severe weather appear to be south of I-66/US-50 across southern MD, 
the VA Piedmont, and northern neck of VA. Damaging winds will be the 
main threat along with locally heavy rainfall. Coverage once again 
will be scattered, but highly dependent on where the front resides 
and if any cloud cover lingers across the region. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning drier this weekend, with increasingly hot 
and humid conditions for early/mid next week.

The late week cold front is expected to stall along the southeastern 
U.S. coastline throughout the weekend. As this occurs, broad surface 
high pressure is likely to extend from the southern Mid-Atlantic up 
to New England. This configuration will support tranquil weather 
this weekend with seasonable temperatures. Mid-level heights (585 to 
589 dm) remain slightly above average which does keep temperatures 
on the warmer side. Humidity levels drop a bit to start the weekend, 
but do begin to come up some as winds shift to southerly on the back 
side of the exiting surface ridge. This eventually sets up for a hot 
and humid period into next week which also marks the conclusion of 
Meteorological Summer (June 1-August 31).

A persistent mid/upper ridge across the southern tier of the country 
is forecast to flex northward in time. Global ensembles generally 
agree on this evolution, but vary with details along the northern 
edge of this ridge. The net result will be another round of hot 
temperatures along with increasing humidity. During the early to mid-
week period, forecast highs rise into the low/mid 90s, with heat 
indices between 98 and 103 degrees. This could inch closer to the 
105 degree heat index mark by Tuesday and Wednesday which is Heat 
Advisory criteria for locations east of the Blue Ridge. Despite all 
of the heat and humidity, daily thunderstorm chances could be more 
limited if the area is underneath the upper ridge. However, these 
details will likely become better resolved in a few days.

Looking a bit further ahead, the Day 6 to 10 outlook from the 
Climate Prediction Center favors above average chances for continued 
heat to linger into subsequent days.

&&

.AVIATION /14Z THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...

VFR conditions will continue to prevail through this evening outside 
of thunderstorms. Some patches of MVFR have been noted north and 
east of BWI/MTN toward LNS/PHL given scattered showers and 
thunderstorms. Biggest threat with the spotty activity this morning 
will be erratic winds, small hail, lightning, and locally heavy 
rainfall. Expect these vicinity storms/showers to continue to pull 
north and east of BWI/MTN over the next 2-3 hrs.

A cold front will approach the region later this afternoon and 
evening before pushing south of the area Friday evening. A few 
strong to severe storms are possible during the afternoon/evening, 
with gusty winds being the primary threat. The timing of storms 
remains a bit uncertain given ongoing convection over northeast MD 
and the placement of surface features that will provide the main 
lift for storms to get going this afternoon. Areas with the highest 
confidence for storms include BWI, IAD, MTN, and MRB with lower
confidence toward DCA and CHO. Went with prevailing 
thunderstorms over these locations given the potential for 
multiple rounds and PROB30s at DCA/CHO. Right now, have storms 
initiating along and west of a line from MRB/HGR to SHD between
18-21z/2-5pm and along the western shore of the bay during this
same time. Eventually activity will shift east likely in a 
broken line between 21-02z/5-10pm. Storms could be slow to push 
through, so there may be some prolonged period of restrictions 
for those that do get storms today. 

Shower and thunderstorm activity may linger into the front half
of the overnight period prior to 6z/2am as the front stalls 
nearby. Some MVFR and IFR cigs and vsbys may develop as a 
result. Current guidance seems to be favor fog, especially west 
of the metro areas. Showers and storms could even redevelop 
Friday, but unsure if this would impact any of the terminals 
(CHO and perhaps DCA would have the highest chances). 

VFR conditions are expected Saturday through Tuesday, which comes 
with a mostly dry forecast. Initial winds will be out of the south 
before an eventual shift to the west by early next week. Relatively 
weak gradients should support peak gusts around 5 to 15 knots.

&&

.MARINE...
Small Craft Advisories remain in effect through 9pm this 
evening for the middle and lower bay as well as lower tidal 
Potomac due to southerly channeling. 

A cold front will approach from the north and west later this 
afternoon and evening bringing the risk of strong 
thunderstorms. Special Marine Warnings will accompany this 
threat, especially later this afternoon and evening. The severe
threat will gradually diminish later this evening and into the 
overnight hours. 

Sub-small craft advisory level winds are expected on Friday as a 
cold front moves in from the northwest. While some additional 
thunderstorms are possible, the greater risk may be south of 
Maryland. Sub-SCA level north to northeasterly winds are forecast 
for Saturday, becoming southerly Sunday as high pressure pushes to 
the east.

While devoid of any discernible convective activity, southerly 
channeling effects could bring areas near Small Craft Advisory 
criteria on Sunday evening into the early overnight period. Winds 
shift to westerly by Monday with a gradual reduction in wind gusts.


&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Increasing southerly flow continues through tonight, leading to
rising water levels. Most locations will only see action 
stages, but Annapolis could approach minor flood stage early 
Thursday morning. With the latest forecast only barely reaching
flood stage, will hold off on an advisory until confidence in
the water level trends increases.

&&
